RagShortTexts: After 1241 devastation, Bela IV and Danylo constructed stone castles and enlisted Cumans.

Variants.Content: After the Mongol invasion of 1241 devastated Hungary, King Béla IV, who is still remembered as the kingdom's second founder, set out to rebuild its defences in stone. He ordered the construction of more than a hundred stone castles, and he settled Cuman horse archers, many of them pagan, on the Alföld plains. Their horses and bows gave the crown a mobile force that could meet raiders on open ground. Fortresses on the hills and along the rivers were meant to hold out when an army could not. In the neighbouring principality of Galicia, King Danylo also built and fortified his towns, including Lviv and Kholm, so that both realms prepared for the next Mongol attack.

Barons invested colossal fortunes into masonry keeps overlooking the Danube and Carpathians. Béla IV proved that while steppe horsemen dominate open grasslands, stone fortifications equipped with siege machinery completely blunt the velocity of nomadic invasions.

Garrisons on the walls of Buda and Visegrád man heavy springalds and ballistas. The steppe tumens cannot forage when royal storehouses sit behind twenty feet of mortar and ashlar stone. A sentry on the keep looks out over the plain each morning, watching for the dust that would mean the horsemen were coming again.

Serfs quarried limestone until hands bled, yet no man cursed the labor. When horsemen descend with torch and lariat, survival means racing cattle across the drawbridge before the iron portcullis drops.
